did_you_know.text: Did you know? Isaiah emphasizes that the LORD is not unable to save or too deaf to hear; the problem does not stem from divine weakness.
Did you know? According to the chapter, it is the people’s sins that create a barrier between them and their God and hide the LORD’s face from them so that he will not hear.
Did you know? The prophet describes sin through parts of the body: hands stained with blood, fingers guilty of wrongdoing, lips speaking lies, and a tongue uttering wickedness.
Did you know? The images of viper’s eggs and spider webs portray destructive acts that offer no real protection: they cannot be turned into clothing to cover those acts.
Did you know? The chapter links injustice with the absence of peace: those who follow sinful ways do not know the way of peace, and their paths are crooked.

Did you know? At this point, the chapter shifts to the first-person plural: the people themselves admit that justice and righteousness are far from them, comparing their condition to a passage from light into darkness.
Did you know? Justice and righteousness are portrayed as withdrawing from society: justice is pushed back, righteousness stands at a distance, and truth is absent from the public square.

Did you know? When the LORD sees that there is no one acting for justice and no one to intercede, he acts himself; the chapter emphasizes that his own arm and righteousness bring salvation and sustain him.
Did you know? Isaiah uses the image of a warrior to portray the LORD’s action: righteousness is his armor, salvation is his helmet, and vengeance and zeal are his clothing.

Did you know? The chapter presents a universal vision: the LORD’s name and glory will be known from west to east, followed by a description of the Redeemer coming to Zion and of the covenant continuing through the generations.
